concepts: constantan resistivity nearly independent of temperature
questions.question: An alloy constantan has resistivity 5 × 10⁻⁷ Ωm at 25°C. If the temperature of this alloy is increased to 50°C then its resistivity will be:
questions.solution: (b) 5 × 10⁻⁷ Ωm. The resistivity of alloys like constantan changes negligibly with temperature.

questions.topic: Energy conversion in a simple pendulum
questions.question:
The diagram shows a pendulum of mass 120 g. A and C are extreme positions and B is the mean position (lowest point); D is a point between B and C; h is the height of C above B. The bob has the velocity 7.5 m/s at B. (g = 10 N/kg)
(1) Which of the following statements is correct?

options.a: At A, the bob has only KE.
options.b: At D, the bob will have more PE and less KE.
options.c: At B, the bob will have only PE.
options.d: At B, the bob will have maximum KE.

questions.solution: (d) At B, the bob will have maximum KE. B is the mean (lowest) position, where speed is maximum.

questions.topic: Conservation of mechanical energy in a pendulum
questions.question:
The diagram shows a pendulum of mass 120 g. A and C are extreme positions and B is the mean position (lowest point); D is a point between B and C; h is the height of C above B. The bob has the velocity 7.5 m/s at B. (g = 10 N/kg)
(2) The height h is:
A machine is said to be efficient, if:

options.a: It produces more energy than it consumes.
options.c: It converts all input energy into useful work.

questions.solution: (c) It converts all input energy into useful work. Efficiency = useful work output / energy input; the closer to 100%, the more efficient.

questions.topic: Free fall and conservation of mechanical energy
concepts: PE converts to KE in free fall
questions.question:
Assertion [A]: The total mechanical energy of a freely falling body is constant.
Reason [R]: Kinetic energy is converted to potential energy as the body falls.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true and R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true but R is false.
options.d: A is false but R is true.

questions.solution: (c) A is true but R is false. Mechanical energy is conserved, but during the fall potential energy is converted into kinetic energy, not the reverse.

questions.question: The wavelength of light in the medium A is 600 nm. The wave enters medium B of refractive index 1.2 with respect to medium A. The wavelength in B is:
questions.solution: (a) 500 nm. Frequency is unchanged, so λ_B = λ_A / ₐn_B = 600/1.2 = 500 nm.

concepts: switch should be in live wire
questions.question:
Assertion [A]: A switch will serve the purpose of making and breaking the circuit when connected to the neutral wire.
Reason [R]: Neutral wire is at zero potential.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct reason for A.
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct reason for A.
options.c: A is true, R is false.
options.d: Both A and R are false.

questions.solution: (b) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct reason for A. A switch in the neutral wire still makes and breaks the circuit (though it is unsafe, as the appliance stays connected to live); this has nothing to do with the neutral wire being at zero potential.

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Principle of moments with metre scale
concepts: weight acts at centre of gravity
questions.question: If the centre of gravity of a metre scale of mass 120 g lies at 45 cm mark, then which one of the following shows the balanced position of the scale? (In each option the fulcrum is at the 60 cm mark and a weight hangs at the 100 cm mark.)

options.a: Fulcrum at 60 cm, 40 gf at 100 cm
options.b: Fulcrum at 60 cm, 45 gf at 100 cm
options.c: Fulcrum at 60 cm, 80 gf at 100 cm
options.d: Fulcrum at 60 cm, 30 gf at 100 cm

questions.solution: (b) 45 gf at the 100 cm mark. Anticlockwise moment of scale's weight = 120 × (60 − 45) = 1800 gf cm; clockwise moment = W × (100 − 60) = 40W, so W = 45 gf.

questions.question: If the frequency of a tuning fork is doubled and its amplitude is halved, the loudness will:
questions.solution: (c) Become one-fourth. Loudness ∝ (amplitude)²; frequency affects pitch, not loudness. (1/2)² = 1/4.

questions.question: A student mixes ice at 0°C with water at 30°C in a calorimeter and notices that some ice remains even after final temperature stabilizes. It indicates:

options.c: Ice has higher SHC than water.

questions.solution: (b) Heat supplied was not enough. The heat given by the water and calorimeter in cooling to 0°C was less than the latent heat needed to melt all the ice.

concepts: refractive index greatest for violet end
questions.question: If red, blue and yellow colour light rays are allowed to enter the same glass block at the same angle of incidence, then for which colour, the value of ∠i − ∠r will be greater?
questions.solution: (d) Blue. Glass has the highest refractive index for blue (of the three), so r is smallest and the deviation (i − r) is greatest.

questions.question: Gamma radiation is dangerous even though its emission doesn't change atomic number or mass as:

options.d: It can penetrate deep into tissues.

questions.solution: (d) It can penetrate deep into tissues. Gamma rays have the highest penetrating power and damage internal organs/cells.

questions.question: The emission which can move the element to the right and down side in the periodic table is:
questions.solution: (b) Beta emission. In β-decay a neutron changes to a proton, so atomic number increases by 1 and the element moves one place to the right in the periodic table.

questions.question: If a lens has power +5 D, what happens when a red and a violet light ray pass through it?
questions.solution: (c) Violet light converges closer. +5 D is a convex lens; its refractive index is greater for violet, so violet is bent more and focuses closer to the lens than red.

questions.topic: Changes in Z and N on alpha and beta decay
questions.question:
The below given graph shows the relation between the number of protons (X axis) and the number of neutrons (Y axis) for the radioactive element Z (not actual symbol) in the periodic table. Z is plotted at 92 protons, 146 neutrons (x-axis 80 to 95, y-axis 140 to 150).
(a) Use graph paper to plot:
(i) The daughter element (label it with W) after the emission of beta radiation by Z.
(ii) The new position of daughter element (label it as H), if W undergoes alpha emission.
questions.solution: Z: protons 92, neutrons 146. (i) β-emission: a neutron changes into a proton, so W has 93 protons and 145 neutrons — plot W at (93, 145). (ii) α-emission from W removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so H has 91 protons and 143 neutrons — plot H at (91, 143).
questions.figure_desc: Grid with protons (80-95) on x-axis and neutrons (140-150) on y-axis, with element Z plotted at about (92, 146).

questions.question:
State the energy conversion in the following:
(a) Bio gas formation
(b) Solar cell
questions.solution:
(a) Bio gas formation: chemical energy stored in biomass (organic waste) is converted into chemical energy of the biogas fuel (by anaerobic decomposition).
(b) Solar cell: light (solar) energy → electrical energy.

marking_points.point: (a) Chemical energy of biomass → chemical energy of biogas

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
concepts: centre of gravity shifts towards added mass
removal of mass shifts CG away
questions.question:
ABCDEF is a regular hexagon with its centre of gravity at O. What will be the most probable position (R, S, T, U, V or O) of the new centre of gravity:
(a) If a small metal washer is glued at point E?
(b) If the hexagon is cut along the line PQ? (of the remaining part ABCDQPF)
questions.solution:
(a) U — the added mass at E shifts the CG from O along OE towards E.
(b) S — removing the triangular part PEQ near E shifts the CG of the remaining part away from E, i.e. upward along EB to S.
questions.figure_desc: Regular hexagon ABCDEF (B at top, E at bottom) with centre O; points R (near A), S (above O on BE), V (right of O), T (lower left), U (below O on OE); line PQ cuts off the bottom vertex E.

questions.question:
Few lenses, made of the same material, are taken as shown below (four biconvex lenses P, Q, R, S of equal height; P is the thinnest, Q the thickest, R and S of intermediate thickness).
(a) Which lens has the maximum power?
(b) Which one has the longest focal length?
questions.solution:
(a) Q — it is the thickest (most curved) lens, so it has the shortest focal length and maximum power.
(b) P — it is the thinnest (least curved), so it has least power and the longest focal length.
questions.figure_desc: Four biconvex lenses P, Q, R, S of the same height drawn side by side; P is thinnest and Q is thickest.

questions.topic: Quality of sound and loudness-amplitude relation
questions.question:
Anshu is playing a flute and Priti is playing a piano for Cascade, at same loudness and pitch.
(a) Name the characteristic that is different for both the instruments.
(b) If, now the loudness of flute increases to four times than before, then compare the amplitudes of the flute and the piano.
questions.solution:
(a) Quality (timbre) — due to different waveforms.
(b) Loudness ∝ A²; 4 times loudness ⇒ amplitude doubles. Amplitude of flute : piano = 2 : 1.

questions.topic: Temperature rise and specific heat capacity
questions.question:
The two metals A and B have their specific heat capacities in the ratio 2:3. If they are supplied same amount of heat, then:
(a) Which metal piece will show a greater rise in temperature, if their masses are the same?
(b) Calculate the ratio in which their temperature rise, if the mass ratio of A to B is 3:5?
questions.solution:
(a) A — for same Q and m, ΔT ∝ 1/c, and A has the lower specific heat capacity.
(b) Q = m_A c_A ΔT_A = m_B c_B ΔT_B ⇒ ΔT_A/ΔT_B = (m_B c_B)/(m_A c_A) = (5 × 3)/(3 × 2) = 15/6 = 5/2. Ratio = 5 : 2.

questions.topic: Total internal reflection in a right-angled prism
concepts: speed of light in glass vs air
questions.question:
The diagram shows the path of a light ray through a right-angled prism ABC of critical angle 42° (∠A = 30°, ∠B = 90°). Ray PQ enters face CB normally at Q, travels parallel to AB and strikes AC at R, is reflected along RS to face AB, and emerges into air along ST.
(a) What is the angle of incidence at the surface AC and AB?
(b) Speed of ray RS is greater than ST. True or False?
questions.solution:
(a) At AC: the ray travels parallel to AB, so it makes 30° with AC; angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60° (> 42°, so total internal reflection). The reflected ray RS then makes 30° with the horizontal and meets the vertical face AB with angle of incidence = 30° (< 42°, so it refracts out along ST).
(b) False — RS is inside glass (denser), where light travels slower than in air (ST).
questions.figure_desc: Right-angled prism with ∠A = 30° at the top and right angle at B; ray PQ enters base CB normally, hits AC at R, reflects to S on AB and emerges as ST.

concepts: cooling curve plateaus = change of state
questions.question:
The figure shows the cooling curve (temperature °C vs time) for a substance Z: part A falls from 180°C to 140°C; part B is flat at 140°C; part C falls from 140°C to 60°C; part D is flat at about 60°C; part E falls below 60°C.
(a) State the temperature at which Z freezes.
(b) What does the part B show?
(c) Mention the temperature range in which the substance is in its liquid state?
(d) What is the boiling point of the substance Z?
questions.solution:
(a) 60°C (second plateau D: liquid → solid).
(b) Part B shows change of state from vapour (gas) to liquid, i.e. condensation at constant temperature 140°C while latent heat is released.
(c) Between 140°C and 60°C (part C).
(d) 140°C.
questions.figure_desc: Cooling curve of Z: falls 180→140°C (A), plateau at 140°C (B), falls to 60°C (C), plateau at 60°C (D), then falls (E).

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Moment of force about a pivot (roller over a kerb)
questions.question: A roller with the diameter of 0.4 m is raised over a pavement AB by applying forces F1 and F2 as shown (the roller of centre O rests against the edge A of the pavement, A being level with O; F2 acts horizontally at the top of the roller and F1 acts vertically upward at the leftmost point of the roller). If F1 = F2 = 20 N, calculate and compare the torques produced by both the forces. (Assuming that both the forces can singularly raise the roller.)
questions.solution:
The roller turns about the edge A of the pavement (radius r = 0.2 m, A level with O).
F2 (horizontal, at top): perpendicular distance from A = r = 0.2 m ⇒ τ₂ = 20 × 0.2 = 4 N m.
F1 (vertical, at leftmost point): perpendicular distance from A = 2r = 0.4 m ⇒ τ₁ = 20 × 0.4 = 8 N m.
τ₁ : τ₂ = 8 : 4 = 2 : 1 — F1 produces twice the torque of F2.
questions.figure_desc: Roller of centre O resting against a pavement edge A level with O (B beyond A); F2 horizontal at the top of the roller, F1 vertically upward at its leftmost point.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Resonance and natural frequency vs length
questions.question:
The diagram shows four plastic balls fitted on wires on a wooden box (wire lengths: D longest, then B, then C, A shortest). Suraj shakes the box forward & backward periodically. He observes that all the balls also start vibrating but one ball vibrates vigorously.
(a) Why does one ball vibrate vigorously?
(b) If all the balls are vibrating with their natural frequency, then arrange the frequencies of all the four balls in increasing order.
(c) Give reason for answer (b).
questions.solution:
(a) Resonance — the natural frequency of that ball (wire) equals the frequency of the periodic force applied by shaking the box, so it vibrates with maximum amplitude.
(b) D < B < C < A.
(c) The natural frequency of vibration decreases as the length of the vibrating wire increases; D has the longest wire and A the shortest.

marking_points.point: (a) Resonance: its natural frequency equals the frequency of shaking

questions.figure_desc: Wooden box with four balls A, B, C, D on vertical wires; D's wire is longest, then B, then C, A shortest.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Energy loss due to friction in pendulum
questions.question:
Two students are conducting an experiment with identical 100 g mass simple pendulums, each raising the bob 5 m above the mean position. The graphs show the relationship between the distance from the mean position and velocities: for student 1 the maximum velocity at the mean position is 10 m/s; for student 2 it is 8 m/s. [g = 10 m/s²]
Using calculations, show which student's experiment saved on the energy lost due to friction.
questions.solution:
PE at extreme = mgh = 0.1 × 10 × 5 = 5 J (same for both).
Student 1: KE at mean = ½ × 0.1 × 10² = 5 J ⇒ energy lost = 5 − 5 = 0 J.
Student 2: KE at mean = ½ × 0.1 × 8² = 3.2 J ⇒ energy lost = 5 − 3.2 = 1.8 J.
Student 1's experiment saved on the energy lost due to friction (no loss).

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Mass of ice to cool water and calorimeter
questions.question:
250 g of water at 30°C is present in a copper calorimeter of mass 50 g. Calculate the mass of ice required to bring down the temperature of calorimeter and its contents to 5°C.
Specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 336 × 10³ J kg⁻¹
Specific heat capacity of copper vessel = 400 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
Specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
questions.solution:
Heat lost by water = 0.25 × 4200 × (30 − 5) = 26250 J.
Heat lost by calorimeter = 0.05 × 400 × 25 = 500 J. Total heat lost = 26750 J.
Heat gained by ice (at 0°C) of mass m = m × 336000 + m × 4200 × (5 − 0) = 357000 m.
357000 m = 26750 ⇒ m = 0.0749 kg ≈ 74.9 g (≈ 75 g).

marking_points.point: Heat lost by water and calorimeter = 26250 + 500 = 26750 J

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Successive alpha and beta decay equations
questions.question: A radioactive nucleus undergoes a series of radiations and emits one beta, one alpha and gamma rays from ᶻX1ᴬ (atomic number Z, mass number A) to form X3 with atomic number 70 and mass number 172. Show these changes in separate equations and find the value of Z and A.
questions.solution:
β-emission: ᴬ_Z X1 → ᴬ_(Z+1) X2 + ⁰₋₁e
α-emission: ᴬ_(Z+1) X2 → ᴬ⁻⁴_(Z−1) X3 + ⁴₂He
γ-emission: ¹⁷²₇₀X3* → ¹⁷²₇₀X3 + γ (no change in A or Z)
Z − 1 = 70 ⇒ Z = 71; A − 4 = 172 ⇒ A = 176.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
Circuit: a 24 V battery is connected across points a and b. Between a and b there are three parallel branches: (1) a 6 Ω resistor with switch S1; (2) 2 Ω and 10 Ω in series with switch S2; (3) a 4 Ω resistor with switch S3.
Which one of the switches S1, S2 or S3 should be opened so that:
(a) The total resistance is equal to 4 Ω.
(b) The total resistance is equal to 3 Ω.
(c) The current through the 4 Ω resistor is 3/5 of the new (with only 2 switches closed) current.
It is mandatory to show all the working.
questions.solution:
Branches: 6 Ω (S1), 12 Ω (S2: 2 + 10), 4 Ω (S3).
(a) Open S3: 6 ∥ 12 = (6 × 12)/18 = 4 Ω.
(b) Open S1: 12 ∥ 4 = 48/16 = 3 Ω.
(c) Current in 4 Ω = 24/4 = 6 A whenever S3 is closed. Open S1: total current = 24/3 = 8 A, 6/8 = 3/4 ✗. Open S2: R = 6 ∥ 4 = 2.4 Ω, total current = 24/2.4 = 10 A, 6/10 = 3/5 ✓. So open S2.

marking_points.point: (c) I(4 Ω) = 6 A; with S2 open R = 2.4 Ω, I = 10 A

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Convex lens image and object at focus
concepts: object at F gives image at infinity
questions.question:
A lens of power +5 D has an object placed at a distance of 50 cm in front of the lens.
(a) State the nature of the image formed.
(b) What is the distance, in exact measurement, towards or away from the lens, the object should move so that the image is not seen.
questions.solution:
f = 1/P = 1/5 m = 20 cm (convex lens). Object at 50 cm is beyond 2F (40 cm).
(a) Image is real, inverted and diminished (formed between F and 2F on the other side; 1/v = 1/20 − 1/50 ⇒ v = 33.3 cm).
(b) The image is not formed (formed at infinity) when the object is at the focus, 20 cm from the lens. So the object must move 50 − 20 = 30 cm towards the lens.

marking_points.point: (b) Object must be at F (image at infinity)

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Principle of moments in a crane
questions.question:
Study the diagram (a crane: a load of 8000 kgf hangs at 25 m from the tower on one side; a 40,000 N force acts at 10 m on the other side, where the worker stands).
(a) In the diagram, is the worker trying to raise or lower the load?
(b) Justify your answer to (a) with the calculations.
questions.solution:
Taking g = 10 N/kg, load = 8000 kgf = 80,000 N.
Moment of load = 80,000 × 25 = 2,000,000 N m (2 × 10⁶ N m).
Moment of the 40,000 N force = 40,000 × 10 = 400,000 N m (4 × 10⁵ N m).
(a) The moment due to the load is greater, so the load side turns down — the worker is lowering the load.
(b) Since 2 × 10⁶ N m > 4 × 10⁵ N m, the arm does not balance in favour of raising; the load descends (is lowered).

marking_points.point: Load moment greater ⇒ load is lowered

questions.figure_desc: Tower crane with arm 25 m on the load side (a vehicle labelled load, 8000 kgf) and 10 m on the other side with a 40,000 N weight and workers.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
concepts: concave lens diverges parallel ray from F
questions.question:
The diagram shows an object PQ kept in front of a lens (beyond 2F). The path of one ray is shown: a ray from P parallel to the principal axis diverges away from the axis after passing through the lens.
(a) Identify and name the lens.
(b) State one use of this kind of image formation.
(c) Redraw and complete the diagram to show the formation of image.
questions.solution:
(a) Concave (diverging) lens — the parallel ray diverges after refraction, appearing to come from the focus on the object side.
(b) Used in a door peephole / to correct myopia (wide field of view with a diminished image).
(c) Diagram: extend the refracted ray backwards (dotted) to pass through F on the object side; draw a second ray from P through the optical centre undeviated. The dotted line and this ray meet between F and the lens, giving image P'Q' — virtual, erect, diminished, on the same side as the object.

marking_points.point: (c) Ray through optical centre and backward extension of refracted ray to F
(c) Virtual, erect, diminished image between F and lens

questions.figure_desc: Object PQ beyond 2F of a lens; a ray from P parallel to the axis bends upward away from the axis after the lens.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
In a prism of angle 60° the angle of minimum deviation for yellow light is 30°.
(a) What is the angle of incidence for this situation?
(b) How will the angle of deviation change, if the angle of prism increases?
questions.solution:
(a) At minimum deviation, i = e and A + δm = i + e = 2i ⇒ 60° + 30° = 2i ⇒ i = 45°.
(b) The angle of deviation increases as the angle of the prism increases.

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Centre of gravity of a composite rod
questions.question: A metre rod is half made of copper and half made of iron. If the mass of the copper part is 900 g and the mass of iron is 800 g, then calculate the position at which the rod can remain in equilibrium. Drawing the figure is necessary.
questions.solution:
Copper part (0–50 cm): 900 gf acting at its centre, 25 cm mark. Iron part (50–100 cm): 800 gf at 75 cm mark.
Let the rod balance at x cm from the copper end. Moments about x: 900 (x − 25) = 800 (75 − x) ⇒ 900x − 22500 = 60000 − 800x ⇒ 1700x = 82500 ⇒ x = 48.5 cm.
The rod balances at the 48.5 cm mark (1.5 cm from the centre, on the copper side). Figure: metre rod with fulcrum at 48.5 cm, 900 gf downward at 25 cm and 800 gf downward at 75 cm.

marking_points.point: Figure with weights at 25 cm and 75 cm and fulcrum

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Block and tackle: VR, MA and efficiency
questions.question:
The diagram shows a Block & Tackle system (upper fixed block with 3 pulleys, lower movable block with 2 pulleys, load hung from the lower block).
(a) Copy and redraw a completely labelled diagram showing the correct connections of the tackle, direction of forces involved to obtain the maximum VR and convenient direction.
(b) Calculate the MA of this system if its efficiency is 80%.
questions.solution:
(a) Tie one end of the string to the hook of the lower (movable) block; pass it alternately over the pulleys of the upper block and under those of the lower block; the free end comes off the last pulley of the upper block with effort E applied downward. Label: upper fixed block, lower movable block, load L (downward), effort E (downward), tension T in each of the 5 segments supporting the lower block (upward).
(b) Number of strands supporting the lower block = 5 ⇒ VR = 5. MA = η × VR = 0.8 × 5 = 4.

marking_points.point: Correct threading (string tied to lower block, effort downward)

questions.figure_desc: Block and tackle: upper fixed block with three pulleys attached to a support and lower movable block with two pulleys carrying the load (string not drawn).

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
The diagram shows a bulb connected by dual control (two-way) switches in two circuits A and B. In A the two traveller wires join top-to-top and bottom-to-bottom (left lever on the top contact, right lever on the bottom contact). In B the traveller wires are crossed (left lever on the top contact, right lever on the bottom contact). In both, the bulb is joined to N, the common terminal of one switch goes to the bulb and the other switch's common terminal goes to L.
(a) Which switch can successfully turn the bulbs ON and OFF? (Circuit A or circuit B or both?)
(b) At present, which bulb is glowing?
(c) If L and N are swapped in the circuit of your answer to the above question, will the circuit work?
questions.solution:
(a) Both — in each circuit the two travellers connect the two-way switches, so either switch can turn the bulb on or off (crossing the travellers only changes which lever positions give ON).
(b) Bulb B — its levers connect through the crossed traveller (top-left to bottom-right), completing the circuit; in A the levers are on different travellers, so the circuit is broken.
(c) Yes, the bulb will still turn ON and OFF, but it is unsafe: the switches would then be in the neutral wire and the bulb would remain connected to the live wire even when switched off.

marking_points.point: (c) Works but unsafe — switch in neutral, bulb stays live

questions.figure_desc: Two dual-control (two-way) switch circuits A and B, each with a bulb between N and the switches; A has parallel traveller wires, B has crossed traveller wires.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.question:
A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 2 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω.
Calculate the current through:
(a) 2 Ω resistor.
(b) 6 Ω resistor.
questions.solution:
6 ∥ 3 = 18/9 = 2 Ω. Total resistance = 2 + 2 + 1 (internal) = 5 Ω.
(a) I = E/(R + r) = 1.5/5 = 0.3 A through the 2 Ω resistor.
(b) p.d. across parallel part = 0.3 × 2 = 0.6 V ⇒ current in 6 Ω = 0.6/6 = 0.1 A.

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Ray path and deviation through a right-angled prism
questions.question:
The figure shows a glass prism ABC of critical angle 42° (∠A = 48°, ∠B = 90°, so ∠C = 42°). A ray QP is incident normally on face AC at P (near A).
(a) Redraw the diagram and complete the path of the light ray PQ till it emerges out of the prism.
(b) Also, calculate the net angle of deviation of the ray PQ when it emerges from the prism.
questions.solution:
(a) The ray enters AC normally and goes undeviated. Since it is perpendicular to AC and AC makes 42° with BC, the ray makes 48° with BC, i.e. meets face AB at an angle of incidence of 48° > 42° ⇒ total internal reflection at AB. The reflected ray travels towards BC and meets it at an angle of incidence of 90° − 48° = 42° = critical angle, so it emerges grazing along the surface BC (angle of refraction 90°).
(b) The incident ray travels at 48° below the horizontal towards AB; the final ray travels along BC towards C. Net deviation = 180° − 48° = 132°.

marking_points.point: At BC i = 42° = C, ray grazes along BC
Correct diagram with arrows and normals

questions.choice_note: any 4 of 6 questions in Section B
concepts: effect of temperature on refractive index
questions.question:
ABC is a glass block whose two sides, AB and BC, are at right angles to each other (AD is a curved face). A ray of light is incident on the surface AB from inside, as shown, and suffers total internal reflection before falling on the surface BC. Finally, the light ray emerges out along the surface BC. The angle between the reflected ray (inside the block) and the face BC (measured towards C) is marked 132°.
(a) What is the angle of incidence at the surface AB?
(b) What is the critical angle for the glass block BC?
(c) What would happen to the critical angle, if the glass block is heated?
questions.solution:
(a) The reflected ray makes 180° − 132° = 48° with BC (and with the normal to AB), so the angle of incidence at AB = 48°.
(b) At BC the angle of incidence = 90° − 48° = 42°; since the ray emerges grazing along BC, the critical angle = 42°.
(c) On heating, the refractive index of glass decreases slightly, so the critical angle increases.
questions.figure_desc: Glass block with face AB on top, BC vertical on the right and curved face AD; a ray totally reflects at AB, strikes BC with 132° marked, and emerges along BC.

questions.chapter: Force: Turning Forces and Uniform Circular Motion
questions.topic: Non-uniform rod and principle of moments
concepts: centre of gravity of non-uniform rod
questions.question:
A metal rod of length 80 cm is balanced at 35 cm from the end A with 100 gf force weights suspended from the two ends (A at 0 cm and B at 80 cm); the centre of the rod is at 40 cm.
(a) If this rod is cut at the centre C then compare the weight of AC to the weight of BC.
(b) Give a reason for your answer in (a).
questions.solution:
(a) Weight of AC is greater than weight of BC.
(b) About the fulcrum (35 cm), the moment of the 100 gf at B (100 × 45) exceeds that at A (100 × 35). For balance, the rod's own weight must give an anticlockwise moment, so its centre of gravity lies on the A side of the fulcrum (left of 35 cm, not at 40 cm). Hence the rod is non-uniform with more mass in part AC.

marking_points.point: (b) Moments of end weights unequal; CG on A side of fulcrum

questions.question: A block and tackle system of pulleys has velocity ratio 4. Calculate the potential energy of the load which has the weight of 100 kgf, lifted by this pulley system to a height of 5 m. [g = 10 m/s²]
